title: Capstone: senior design review
objective: Review a new design the way a senior engineer would, with no hints: find the risks, rank them by harm, and choose what to fix first.

sources.title: Stripe: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency
IETF RFC 6585: HTTP status code 429 Too Many Requests

simplifies: A made-up system for practice, not any company's. Request rates, costs and timings are illustrative. A real review would also cover security, privacy and cost in more depth.

steps.caption: The brief: an AI support assistant for an online shop. Customers ask about orders; the assistant answers, and can issue refunds. Expected load (illustrative): a few thousand chats an hour, with spikes after big sales.
The proposal, part 1: every customer message calls the model API and waits for the answer, with no timeout. The full chat history is sent on every call.
Part 2: to answer "where's my order?", the assistant runs a query over the orders database, built from the customer's text by the model.
Part 3: when the model decides a refund is fair, the assistant calls the refund service directly, with no limit on the amount and no human check. If the call times out, it calls again.
Part 4: if the model API returns 429 (too many requests), the assistant retries straight away until it works. All chats share one API key.
Your turn. Some of these choices are fine; several are not. There are no hints in this review: weigh each part against what you've learned about failure, retries, load and safety.

critique.prompt: Review the proposal you just stepped through. Tap every real risk.

risks.text: Refunds have no limit and no human check, so a wrong or manipulated model decision pays out real money
risks.why: Cap automatic refunds and send larger ones to a person for approval.

risks.text: Retrying a refund that timed out can pay it twice
risks.why: Send an idempotency key with each refund, so a retry returns the first result.

risks.text: Running a database query built by the model from customer text lets a customer steer the query
risks.why: Give the assistant a fixed lookup (orders for this signed-in customer), not free-form queries.

risks.text: Retrying straight away on 429, with one shared key, keeps the limit exhausted for every chat
risks.why: Back off with jitter, and queue or shed load when the limit is reached.

risks.text: No timeout on the model call lets one slow response tie up the chat, and many slow ones tie up the service
risks.why: Set a timeout and show a friendly fallback.

risks.text: The assistant answers order questions automatically
risks.why: That's the point of the product.

risks.text: Customers can ask in their own words
risks.why: Free-text questions are fine; the risk is turning that text into database queries.

critique.hint: Not quite. There are no hints in the capstone: go back over each choice in the proposal and check your picks again.

options.explanation: It can take the assistant down, but nothing is lost permanently.

options.text: The unlimited refunds with no human check
options.explanation: Right. It loses real money, can be triggered on purpose by a manipulative customer, and can't be undone.
Real, but it causes slowness, not lost money.
Serious, but capping the money that can leave comes first.

critique.explain: Rank by harm and reversibility: money paid out wrongly is lost for good. Next, make refunds idempotent and replace free-form queries with fixed lookups, then add timeouts and backoff so overload degrades gracefully.

quiz.prompt: In a design review, how should risks be ranked?

options.text: By harm: what's lost or broken, how many people it affects, and whether it can be undone
options.explanation: Right. Money lost or data broken beats inconvenience.

options.text: By how easy they are to fix
options.explanation: Easy fixes are nice, but the worst risks come first.

options.text: In the order they appear in the design
options.explanation: Order of appearance says nothing about harm.

quiz.prompt: Why is "no timeout" on a call to another service a risk?

options.explanation: A timeout only stops a call that's already too slow.

options.text: It isn't: waiting longer is always safer
options.explanation: Waiting forever ties up resources and users.

options.text: If that service hangs, every request waiting on it hangs too, and they pile up
options.explanation: Right. A timeout turns a hang into a quick failure you can handle.
